questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: Since I am a student of French culture who never had the chance to learn French in school, I wanted to go abroad to improve my skills in oral French. I chose Perpignan because it is a rather small city, at least compared to most other opportunities I was given in choice of destination. I thought that people here would be more laid-back, have more time and patience to listen to my broken French and be less international and thus less likely to speak English. Secondly, being from Denmark and suffering from mild depression during the winter months because of the cold and the general darkness, I found the warm weather, the high number of sunshine hours and the geographical situation of the city appealing. After all, why go to Calais, Normandie or any other département that looks quite like Denmark when you can try out something completely different down South.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It has been great. My spoken French has improved significantly, and I have learned to not love another educational system, which really makes me appreciate where I come from. Since I am older than most of the other students here, and since I have aldready travelled a lot it has not been "the best time of my life" as some people find it, but I am fine with that and did not expect it to be otherwise. I think one thing that could have improved my stay would have been doing it outside of the last covid restrictions - wearing a mask made it difficult to bond with the French students in my class since the absence of facial expressions and the muffling of spoken words made communication difficult, but of course all that was out of the control of the host university or anyone in power.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer:
0!
Information was scarce, classes started before I had even recieved any information concerning anything - my schedule, how to find the class hours, even the first meeting with the person responsible for informing the exchange students. And for accommodation I recieved zero information in advance, and not knowing that nothing was included, I ended up spending the first few nights freezing without any sort of cover.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I had to book a meeting with our contact person, who told me how to find my courses online, gave me a map and promised me a tour of the campus, something that she forgot to to. As for everything else, I had to myself track down other exchange students on campus to be invited groups on social media and actually find other friends in my situation, I had to go through endless procedures to be inscribed into courses, and as a result I missed the three first séances for some courses despite proactively trying my hardest to get into contact with the responsible teachers. All while trying to catch up with the missed classes I, and the rest of the Erasmus students, had to sort out the genuine ocean of administrative inscriptions, tasks and so what all on our own, while being threatened with being kicked out of our accommodations and the university for not having done things that noone had told us to do, or how to do it. In general the first month of the exchange was a glorious administrative mess.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: We were offered to stay in the logement universitaire. Some of the houses are newly constructed and in fine condition, while some of them are rather newly constructed and in terrible condition - I myself came to a block where the kitchen was often closed off and where the stoves often did not work, where noise is a serious problem between 10 PM and 4 AM, and where the rooms are infested with bedbugs and cockroaches. I have also been living with mold since day one.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: Nothing. You even had to buy all your cutleries yourself. While we in my kitchen has a strong culture of sharing a little of the food we cook, this is not the norm.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer: Bring a sleeping bag or something else to get through your first nights. And if you want to stay clear of bugs and fungi, express a strong desire to stay in bâtiment A or B. And also be prepared to spend some time shopping for all things cooking and eating - B&M is a 30 minutes walk from home, and they have everything you need.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: I had to book a meeting with our contact person, who told me how to find my courses online, gave me a map and promised me a tour of the campus, something that she forgot to to. Also you had to fill out a whole lot of papers with her.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Very little. You could write an email to the contact person for Erasmus, but more often than not the reply was not of any help.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Successful, eventually. Being registered was sometimes as easy as talking to the professor, sometimes more difficult, the worst case being my course of introduction to theater, where I missed the first class because it was not possible to be informed of the schedules before courses had started, and then the teacher got sick and made the courses online. But, since I could not meet her, thus not get registered, I did not recieve the zoom link for the courses. In the end I have missed half classes, and it is the one course that I might not have passed for the exams.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Courage! Eventyally you'll get there.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: In general licence 1 and licence 2, with a few outliers from licence 3

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Some of the courses were interesting, but in general I found the way that courses are taught here are inefficient and a huge waste of everyones time. With a slightly bigger focus on self study and the course material being openly available for the students instead of being hidden information that only the teacher can access and the students have to hand copy, I feel that half of the courses I have taken could have been taught within a few lessons.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: All the courses were interesting, at least for me being a student of culture from a country where the litterary tradition is not nearly as old or as wide in its scope.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Mhh, the fact that I needed insurance in order to actually rent my room

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
You can get super cheap bicycles at la casa bicicletta. Most of the erasmus students did not get bikes, and they did indeed commit a grave mistake in not doing so - while buses are cheap they are far in between. With the bike I can go anywhere and often arrive earlier than my friends, I can explore town and have found amazing locations that they would never encounter, I have driven all around the area visiting small idyllic villages and historical sights, or just sped though the wineyards, feeling the warm air against my skin. Alors, students - get yourself a bike!!!!!!
Secondly, although public transport within the city is not well developed, the département has bus lines that take you to most major sites for just one euro! Not that's cheap!

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: There wre a multitude of sports events available! Great.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Many sports, and also more special trips like ski trips, canyoning, etc.
Then there were festivals, concerts, a color run, and so on.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Do some sports, it's a great way to meet people.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Visit smaller villages, go hiking or skiing in the mountains, go to the sea, swim in the river (event if it's not permitted), go to the movies (it's 3 euros for holders of passe culturelle - which is free for erasmus students), or just bask in the sun with your friends.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: It was fine.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Not many, I never got too close to them, but that might have been due to masks being worn, making socializing in a language that you don't know well quite difficult, and my study program, which did not include group work. Some of my friend have met a lot of local friends through group work in classes, so I guess you're okay if you are not a student of lettres.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: It seems that both "no" and "yes" means "maybe" when pronounced by someone French. And that if it is normal in your culture to be less outspoken, they will probably not understand it when you reject them or their ideas.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: People are quite talkative and friendly.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Some of the teachers are predators
Your inscriptions will take time
Be prepared for a cramping writing hand.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer:
La casa bicicletta is where you get your bike for 50 euros AAND a free-to-use workshop with guidance on how to fix your bike when it breaks.
Speak French from day 1

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Meeting a lot of Africans in my kitchen. The thing I appreciate the most about the French language is the fact that it is super international, and thus a key to interact with and to better understand a lot of different cultures.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Surviving the administration and the school system with your sanity intact. That might be an overstatement, but the system seems completely outdated, and the few professors that has taught outside of France that I had did indeed agree with me.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
